trails.trailTip: No permit is needed for the bottom-up day hike from the Temple of Sinawava (you can go as far as Big Spring), but always check the current Flash Flood Potential rating at a visitor center first and turn back at any sign of rising, muddy water.
trails.didYouKnow: The Narrows follows the Virgin River through a gorge that in places is only 20-30 feet wide with walls up to 2,000 feet tall.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round (chains can ice over in winter)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, a lottery permit from Recreation.gov is required for the final chain section from Scout Lookout to the summit — apply in the seasonal lottery (e.g., spring window Feb 13-25 for Mar-May dates) or the day-before lottery (12:01 a.m.-3 p.m. Mountain Time); the approach to Scout Lookout itself needs no permit.
trails.didYouKnow: The Angels Landing permit pilot program began in 2022 after the park was issuing over 200,000 hikers a year onto the narrow chained section.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round (waterfalls best after spring runoff or rain)
trails.trailTip: The rock near the pools and behind the waterfall spray is often slick even when dry-looking — the Upper Pool viewpoint especially rewards slow, careful footing.
trails.didYouKnow: The three Emerald Pools sit at different elevations and are connected by a short but sometimes-closed connector trail depending on rockfall conditions.

trails.trailTip: This paved path is fully accessible and is the easiest way to see the canyon narrows without wading — it ends where the maintained trail stops and the river hike begins.
trails.didYouKnow: The Riverside Walk was built along an old wagon road bed used before Zion Canyon's scenic drive existed.

trails.trailTip: The small trailhead lot just east of the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel fills quickly — some sections along the route hug an unguarded drop-off, so keep kids close.
trails.didYouKnow: The overlook gives one of the only views looking back down into lower Zion Canyon from above, framing the Towers of the Virgin.

trails.bestSeason: Late spring-fall (Lava Point access road closes in winter)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, day hiking the West Rim Trail requires no permit, but an overnight Wilderness Permit is required to camp at any of its 9 designated sites between Lava Point and the Grotto.
trails.didYouKnow: Most thru-hikers arrange a shuttle to the Lava Point trailhead and hike downhill into the canyon, finishing near Angels Landing.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, the classic Weeping Rock route to Observation Point remains closed due to rockfall damage — the only current access is via the East Mesa Trail, which is actually an easier approach than the old route.
trails.didYouKnow: At 6,507 feet, Observation Point looks down on Angels Landing from nearly 700 feet above it.

trails.trailTip: The trail has almost no shade — hike early morning or in the two hours before sunset in summer, and carry more water than for a typical 3-mile hike.
trails.didYouKnow: The Watchman formation is not named for a person but for its resemblance to a lookout tower standing guard over the canyon mouth.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS, day hiking to Kolob Arch requires no permit, but overnight camping along La Verkin Creek is limited to designated sites and requires a Wilderness Permit reserved through Recreation.gov or the visitor center wilderness desk.
trails.didYouKnow: Kolob Arch's exact span has been re-measured over the years and is now generally cited around 287 feet, making it one of the longest freestanding natural arches on Earth.

animals.whereToLook: Steep canyon walls near the East Entrance and Route 9 switchbacks
animals.viewingTip: View from pullouts with binoculars — during the fall rut, rams are focused on each other and easily stressed by close approach, so keep vehicles and viewing distance well back from the road shoulder.
animals.didYouKnow: Desert bighorn were reintroduced to Zion in the 1970s after being extirpated from the area decades earlier.

animals.whereToLook: Zion Canyon floor near the Grotto and Zion Lodge
animals.viewingTip: Deer here are habituated to people but still wild — watch from a few car-lengths away and never feed them, even when they approach picnic areas.
animals.didYouKnow: Mule deer get their name from their oversized, mule-like ears, which rotate independently to pinpoint sound.

animals.whereToLook: High cliffs and thermals above Angels Landing and Zion Canyon
animals.viewingTip: Scan the sky with binoculars for their wing tags and huge wingspan rather than approaching any cliffside roost — condors are critically endangered and extremely sensitive to disturbance near nest and roost sites.
animals.didYouKnow: Every wild California condor wears numbered wing tags as part of an intensive recovery program that began with fewer than 30 birds left in the world in the 1980s.

animals.whereToLook: Seasonal pools and seeps near the Narrows and Emerald Pools
animals.viewingTip: Look, don't touch — handling can transfer oils and pathogens harmful to amphibians, so photograph them in place rather than picking them up.
animals.didYouKnow: Its mottled gray-brown skin is so well camouflaged against sandstone that its call is often the only clue it's nearby.

animals.whereToLook: Sunny slickrock along the Canyon Overlook and Watchman trails
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy from a few feet away with a zoom lens — cornering or grabbing one to get a photo stresses the animal and can cause it to drop its tail.
animals.didYouKnow: Collared lizards can run on their hind legs alone when sprinting after prey.

animals.whereToLook: High plateaus above the main canyon
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are rare and usually brief — if you see one, do not approach; back away slowly, make yourself look large, and give it a clear escape route.
animals.didYouKnow: Mountain lions in Zion's plateau country roam huge territories and are rarely seen despite being one of the park's top predators.

animals.whereToLook: Canyon floor near the Virgin River and campgrounds
animals.viewingTip: Watch from a distance and never feed them — turkeys that associate people with food can become aggressive around picnic areas.
animals.didYouKnow: Wild turkeys can fly in short bursts up to 55 mph despite their bulky appearance.

animals.whereToLook: Canyon walls and rock crevices near campgrounds after dark
animals.viewingTip: If you spot one at night, use a red-filtered flashlight and keep your distance rather than approaching its crevice or den — ringtails are shy and easily driven off from good denning spots.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite the name, ringtails are not cats but relatives of raccoons, with ankles that rotate 180 degrees for climbing sheer rock.

animals.whereToLook: Canyon rim thermals above the main canyon
animals.viewingTip: Watch soaring eagles from canyon-floor overlooks with binoculars rather than trying to get closer to a rim nest site.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles can spot a rabbit from over a mile away thanks to eyesight roughly four to eight times sharper than a human's.
